title: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
word: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
hook: the night begins in the morning, with a little water in the palm and a resolve said out loud
carry: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
tomorrow: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum

segments.voice: Yesterday began Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum: its shape. A fast, worship, staying awake until dawn, and the night itself as the point. What did the dark give back to you? Today, the first lesson. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-four.

The great night of Shiva starts in daylight. Early on the morning of Shivaratri, after a bath, someone who means to keep the night takes a little water into the cupped right palm. They say, out loud or under the breath, where they are, what day it is, who they are, and what they are about to do: I will keep this fast, I will keep this night. Then they let the water go. That's all. A few words and a palmful of water. But everything that happens later, at midnight, at three in the morning, when the body is begging for food and sleep, leans on those few words said in the light. The course doesn't begin with the dark. It begins with signing up.
screen: `WATER IN THE CUPPED PALM.` → `I WILL KEEP THIS NIGHT.` → `THE COURSE BEGINS BY SIGNING UP.`

segments.voice: That moment has a name: sankalpa, a resolve, an intention made on purpose. And the thing it begins is a vrata, a vow kept for a set time. In the Shiva Purana's telling of the Shivaratri vow, the devotee rises early, bathes, and takes the vow before the fast and the vigil begin. Why make the decision so early? Because the hours you'll need it are the hours you can't decide well. At two in the morning almost any reason to quit sounds wise. So the tradition puts the deciding in daylight, when the mind is clear, and lets the night simply carry it out. The water helps too. Words alone can float away. Water poured out of your hand can't be poured back. The resolve becomes something the body did, not just something the mouth said. Behind it sits an old idea. The Chandogya Upanishad says a person is made of resolve: as you resolve in this world, so you become. A sankalpa is that idea, shrunk to one day. And a vow is personal. People who keep Shivaratri don't all take the same one. Some fast completely. Some take only fruit and milk. Some keep the whole night in a temple, some keep part of it at home. The vow that counts is the one you actually said. So the first lesson of the night curriculum isn't hunger or darkness. It's honesty about what you'll do, said clearly enough that you can hold yourself to it later. A night with no resolve at the start is just a late night. A night that was promised in the morning becomes a practice.
screen: `SANKALPA: A RESOLVE.` · `DECIDE IN DAYLIGHT.` · `WATER CAN'T BE POURED BACK.` · `THE VOW YOU ACTUALLY SAID.` · then, large: `AS YOU RESOLVE, SO YOU BECOME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a small sankalpa. Settle, and breathe. Choose one honest thing you'll do before tomorrow: a meal eaten slowly, ten minutes without the phone, a call you've been avoiding. Make it small enough that you'll really keep it. If you have a glass of water nearby, take a little into your palm. Say the resolve quietly to yourself, with where you are and what day it is. Then let the water go, into a plant, a sink, the ground. Sit with what you've promised. If you pray, you can offer the resolve to Shiva, or to the God you know. The bell holds the time.
Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum. Lesson one: the sankalpa, the resolve made in the morning, with water in the palm, that carries the vow through the dark.
Your line: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum. Today, when the moment comes to quit your small resolve, remember you decided it in daylight. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: Hindus keeping Maha Shivaratri may begin the day with a bath and a sankalpa, stating their intention to keep the fast and the vigil; a priest may lead the sankalpa before a temple puja.

fork.setup: it's the morning of Maha Shivaratri. you're not sure you can last the whole night without food. what do you do?
options: skip the vow, since you might fail.
take a vow you can really keep, and say it clearly.
promise everything and hope for the best.
fork.reveal: vows differ from person to person. the night curriculum starts with honesty: the vow that counts is the one you actually said, and then kept.

original.note: Sanskrit: sankalpa, a resolve or intention made on purpose.

notes: Shivaratri day 2 of 7: the sankalpa. Confirm the Shiva Purana passage has the devotee rising early, bathing and taking the vow on the morning of Shivaratri.
The sankalpa form (water in the right palm, stating place, date, name and purpose, then releasing the water) is described as one form; confirm the description and that 'cupped right palm' is fair.
Chandogya 3.14.1 (kratumayah purushah...) paraphrased; Max Müller renders kratu as 'will'. 'Resolve' chosen as a fair gloss; confirm.
Variation in vows (full fast, fruit and milk, part of the night) is stated as practice without numbers; confirm.
